about: The real recent level (2024, or the latest year measured) of each place outcome, per state, D.C. and Puerto Rico where measured. The world starts each place here, and the outcome web moves it from there as laws and conditions change. A place not listed has no base and records nothing, which is unknown and never zero. Values are percents. After the first month nothing pulls a place back to its base: each outcome's underlying level drifts (part national, part the state's own), and now and then a society-wide wave moves it a long way. Laws and conditions act on top, through the outcome web. Drift sizes are PROVISIONAL game values, set so a decade moves a place about as far as recent decades moved real states, and filed for research as society-wide-waves-causes-pace-scale. A measure with scale "index" is a level where 100 is where the place began; it drifts in logs rather than log-odds and scales the outcome it feeds. A measure with scale "rate" is a level in its own unit (violent crimes per 100,000 people, micrograms per cubic meter); it drifts in logs like an index, and its bounds are in that unit.

health.uninsured-pct.name: Share of people without health insurance
health.uninsured-pct.unit: percent of the civilian noninstitutionalized population
health.uninsured-pct.source: U.S. Census Bureau, ACS brief ACSBR-024, Health Insurance Coverage by State: 2023 and 2024, Appendix Table 2 (2024 column).

household.poverty-pct.name: Share of people below the poverty line
household.poverty-pct.unit: percent of people for whom poverty status is determined
household.poverty-pct.source: U.S. Census Bureau, ACS brief ACSBR-026, Poverty in States and Metropolitan Areas: 2024, Table 1 (below 0.50 plus 0.50 to 0.99 of the poverty threshold).
household.poverty-pct.note: The official measure: cash income before taxes. Tax credits and non-cash help (SNAP, housing, Medicaid) do not count, so links from them belong on a supplemental poverty measure, not this one.

school.graduation-pct.name: Share of public high school students who graduate on time
school.graduation-pct.unit: percent of the four-year adjusted cohort
school.graduation-pct.source: NCES Digest of Education Statistics 2023, Table 219.46: four-year adjusted cohort graduation rate, 2021-22 (New Mexico and Oklahoma 2020-21, the latest they reported).

school.math-proficient-pct.name: Share of eighth graders proficient in math
school.math-proficient-pct.unit: percent at or above NAEP Proficient, grade 8 mathematics
school.math-proficient-pct.source: National Assessment of Educational Progress 2024, grade 8 mathematics, percent at or above Proficient (NAEP Data Service).

voting.turnout-pct.name: Share of eligible voters who voted in a presidential election
voting.turnout-pct.unit: percent of the voting-eligible population, total ballots counted
voting.turnout-pct.source: University of Florida Election Lab, 2024 General Election Turnout v0.4 (VEP turnout rate).

births.rate-index.name: How many babies are born against where the place began
births.rate-index.source: Starts at 100 everywhere; drift is sized to the U.S. record (fertility down about 20% from 2007 to 2023; the baby boom and bust moved it far more).

crime.violent.name: Violent crimes per 100,000 people
crime.violent.unit: violent crimes known to police per 100,000 residents (murder and nonnegligent manslaughter, rape, robbery, aggravated assault)
crime.violent.source: FBI Crime Data Explorer, 2024: the sum of the 12 monthly violent crime rates for reporting agencies in each state (https://cde.ucr.cjis.gov/LATEST/summarized/state/{ST}/violent-crime?from=01-2024&to=12-2024&type=rates), read by CLOUD I on Sept. 28, 2026. These cover the population the reporting agencies serve (96% nationally), so they run 1 to 4% above the FBI's estimated state totals.
crime.violent.note: The state's one crime level: it replaces the old crime index at 100, and town crime reads it as a ratio to where the state began. Puerto Rico's reported 15.2 is not believable and the Virgin Islands reported nothing, so both are unknown.

housing.homelessness.name: People homeless per 10,000 people
housing.homelessness.unit: people experiencing homelessness on one night in January per 10,000 residents (point-in-time count)
housing.homelessness.source: HUD, 2024 Annual Homelessness Assessment Report Part 1, Appendix A, people experiencing homelessness per 10,000 (https://www.huduser.gov/portal/sites/default/files/pdf/2024-AHAR-Part-1.pdf), whole numbers as HUD rounds them. Puerto Rico, Guam and the Virgin Islands: HUD's 2024 counts (2007-2024 PIT Counts by State, https://www.huduser.gov/portal/sites/default/files/xls/2007-2024-PIT-Counts-by-State.xlsb) over the Census Vintage 2024 population for Puerto Rico and the 2020 Census count for Guam and the Virgin Islands.
housing.homelessness.note: American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands have no HUD count, so they are unknown.

env.particulates.name: Fine particles in the air
env.particulates.unit: population-weighted annual average fine particulate matter (PM2.5), micrograms per cubic meter
env.particulates.source: America's Health Rankings, Air Pollution, from EPA data, 2022-2024 (https://www.americashealthrankings.org/explore/measures/air), read by CLOUD I on Sept. 28, 2026. U.S. 8.8.

env.drinking-water-violations.name: Drinking-water health violations per water system
env.drinking-water-violations.unit: health-based drinking-water violations per community water system in a year
env.drinking-water-violations.source: America's Health Rankings, Drinking Water Violations, from EPA's Safe Drinking Water Information System, 2024 (https://www.americashealthrankings.org/explore/measures/hb_water_violation), read by CLOUD I on Sept. 28, 2026. U.S. 2.5.
env.drinking-water-violations.note: Hawaii measured 0. A level that drifts in logs cannot start at zero, so Hawaii starts at 0.05; the floor sits lower (0.01) so its level can drift down as well as up.

household.food-insecurity.name: Share of households that are food insecure
household.food-insecurity.source: USDA ERS, Household Food Security in the United States in 2024 (ERR-358), Table 5 (2022-2024 average; matches CLOUD I's Table 4 check), https://www.ers.usda.gov/media/9161/err-358.pdf

school.reading-proficient-pct.name: Share of eighth graders proficient in reading
school.reading-proficient-pct.unit: percent at or above NAEP Proficient, grade 8 reading
school.reading-proficient-pct.source: NAEP Data Service, 2024 grade 8 reading, ALC:AP, https://www.nationsreportcard.gov/DataService/GetAdhocData.aspx?type=data&subject=reading&grade=8&subscale=RRPCM&variable=TOTAL&stattype=ALC:AP&Year=2024 (Puerto Rico not displayable)

school.college-completion-pct.name: Share of adults 25 and older with a bachelor's degree or more
school.college-completion-pct.note: Drift is slow: the adult population's attainment changes a few tenths of a point a year.

broadband.home-access.name: Share of households with a broadband subscription
broadband.home-access.source: ACS 2024 1-year, S2801_C02_014E (broadband of any type), via https://data.census.gov/api/access/data/table?id=ACSST1Y2024.S2801

health.child-asthma-pct.name: Share of children with current asthma
health.child-asthma-pct.source: National Survey of Children's Health 2022 and 2023 topical files (Census), K2Q40A and K2Q40B, weighted by FWC, the two years pooled at half weight each; national 6.6%. https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/nsch/datasets/

health.overdose-deaths.name: Drug overdose deaths per 100,000 people
health.overdose-deaths.source: CDC VSRR provisional drug overdose death counts, 12 months ending December 2024 (data.cdc.gov xkb8-kh2a; New York adds New York City), over ACS 2024 total population (DP05_0001E); national 23.6
health.overdose-deaths.note: Crude rate (not age-adjusted): 12-month provisional counts ending December 2024 over the 2024 population.

labor.median-earnings.name: Median earnings of people with earnings
labor.median-earnings.unit: 2024 dollars a year, people 16 and older with earnings

transit.service-access.name: Transit service per resident
transit.service-access.unit: vehicle revenue miles per resident a year
transit.service-access.source: FTA National Transit Database 2024 (data.transportation.gov ekg5-frzt, summed by the reporting agency's state) over ACS 2024 population. D.C.'s 224.8 counts WMATA's whole regional service.
transit.service-access.note: Service counts toward the state where the reporting agency is based, so D.C.'s figure includes WMATA's service in Maryland and Virginia.

transit.ridership.name: Transit rides per resident
transit.ridership.unit: unlinked passenger trips per resident a year
transit.ridership.source: FTA National Transit Database 2024 (data.transportation.gov ekg5-frzt, unlinked passenger trips summed by the reporting agency's state) over the Census Bureau's July 1, 2024 population estimate (NST-EST2024-ALLDATA). Nationally 7.66 billion trips, 22.5 per resident of the 50 states and D.C.
transit.ridership.note: Trips count toward the state where the reporting agency is based, so D.C.'s 377.2 includes WMATA's riders from Maryland and Virginia. Guam, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands report to the database but are left out, as in transit service, because the Census Bureau publishes no 2024 estimate for them. The drift is judged, like transit service's.

gov.borrowing-cost.name: What a state pays to borrow, over the best-rated states
gov.borrowing-cost.unit: basis points over a AAA-rated state on general-obligation bonds
gov.borrowing-cost.source: S&P general-obligation ratings for 2024 (Wikipedia, List of U.S. states by credit rating, from S&P Global; D.C. from its current S&P rating; Montana from Moody's Aa1, as S&P does not rate it), priced at 6 basis points per notch below AAA through A+ (Joffe, Doubly Bound: The Cost of Issuing Municipal Bonds, Haas Institute 2017, from Bloomberg five-year index yields), and 12 per notch below A+, where the same source says spreads steepen (the 12 is this game's reading, not the source's number)
gov.borrowing-cost.note: Puerto Rico and the territories are unknown. A AAA state starts at 0 and may drift a little below it, as top-rated bonds sometimes trade through the benchmark.

population.in-migration.name: People moving into the state each year, per 1,000
population.in-migration.unit: people moving in per 1,000 people on tax returns a year
population.in-migration.source: IRS Statistics of Income, state-to-state migration data, 2022 to 2023 (stateinflow2223.csv and stateoutflow2223.csv, total migration, U.S. and foreign), people on returns (n2)
population.in-migration.note: Per 1,000 people on tax returns filed in the state at the end of the year; tax filers only, so people who file no return are missing. Net migration is in-migration minus out-migration.

population.out-migration.name: People moving out of the state each year, per 1,000
population.out-migration.unit: people moving out per 1,000 people on tax returns a year
population.out-migration.source: IRS Statistics of Income, state-to-state migration data, 2022 to 2023 (stateinflow2223.csv and stateoutflow2223.csv, total migration, U.S. and foreign), people on returns (n2)
population.out-migration.note: Per 1,000 people on tax returns filed in the state at the start of the year; tax filers only.

program.snap-receipt.name: Share of residents receiving SNAP
program.snap-receipt.source: USDA FNS SNAP Data Tables, National Data Bank version 8.2: FY 2024 average monthly persons participating by state (FY24.xlsx in https://fns-prod.azureedge.us/sites/default/files/resource-files/snap-zip-fy69tocurrent-9.zip), over the Census Bureau's July 1, 2024 population estimate (NST-EST2024-ALLDATA); Guam and the U.S. Virgin Islands over their 2020 Census counts (153,836 and 87,146), since the Census Bureau publishes no 2024 estimate for the island areas; national (50 states and D.C.) 12.3
program.snap-receipt.note: Puerto Rico, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands run a Nutrition Assistance Program block grant instead of SNAP, so they record nothing here. The monthly drift and bounds are judged, as for food insecurity, not read from the year-to-year series.

finance.high-cost-loans.name: Consumer lending storefronts per 100,000 residents
finance.high-cost-loans.unit: establishments whose main business is consumer lending (payday, title and installment lenders) per 100,000 residents
finance.high-cost-loans.source: Census Bureau County Business Patterns 2023, state file (https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/cbp/datasets/2023/cbp23st.zip), establishments in NAICS 522291 (consumer lending), over the American Community Survey 2024 5-year total population, table B01003 (https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b01003.dat). 12,104 establishments across 49 states and D.C.: 3.6 per 100,000 residents.
finance.high-cost-loans.note: Storefront lenders stand in for high-cost borrowing, because no agency counts high-cost loans by state; the establishment count is the closest measured fact and the McKernan-Ratcliffe-Kuehn effect is measured on the same kind of use. Alaska and Vermont are left out because the Census Bureau withholds their consumer-lending count, and Puerto Rico and the other territories because County Business Patterns does not cover them; those places are unknown and never zero. The drift is judged.

env.container-recycling-pct.name: Share of beverage containers recycled
env.container-recycling-pct.source: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: Container Recycling Institute (container-recycling.org/bottle-bills), states with a container deposit law return 71.6% of beverage containers and states without one 27.9% (BEAR 2002, quoted in its Bottle Bill Resource Guide); each place takes its group's average by the deposit law it began with (data/research/laws/starting-law-2026.json), since state-by-state recycling rates were not read

household.prices.name: Consumer price level
household.prices.unit: price level for all consumer goods and services relative to the U.S. average, which is 100 (regional price parity)
household.prices.source: Bureau of Economic Analysis, Regional Price Parities by State, 2024, all items (SARPP line 1, https://apps.bea.gov/regional/zip/SARPP.zip, released February 11, 2026). Nationally 100 by construction: a state at 110.7 (California) pays 10.7% more than the U.S. average for the same goods and services, one at 86.9 (Arkansas) 13.1% less.
household.prices.note: A price level against the nation, not a rate of inflation: the outcome web moves a state's level up or down from where the law leaves it, so a tariff changes what a household pays there. D.C. is included. Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands are outside the regional price parities and are unknown, never zero. The drift keeps the earlier judged settings and is not measured; a state's level against the nation moves a point or two a year.

health.drug-out-of-pocket.name: What Medicare enrollees pay out of pocket for drugs
health.drug-out-of-pocket.unit: mean Part D out-of-pocket drug spending per enrollee in 2022, dollars a year (all enrollees, low-income subsidy and not)
health.drug-out-of-pocket.source: HHS Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation, Inflation Reduction Act Research Series: Medicare Part D Enrollee Out-of-Pocket Spending (January 2024), Table 6, Part D annual out-of-pocket spending for enrollees by state in 2022, total (non-LIS and LIS) mean (https://aspe.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/documents/1b652899fb99dd7e6e0edebbcc917cc8/aspe-part-d-oop.pdf). 52.4 million enrollees in the 50 states and D.C., an enrollment-weighted mean of $352.
health.drug-out-of-pocket.note: The reading is 2022, before the Inflation Reduction Act's Part D changes began in 2023 and the out-of-pocket cap in 2025, so a state starts above what enrollees pay today until a law or the drift moves it. Puerto Rico and the other territories are not in the table and are unknown, never zero. The drift keeps the earlier judged settings and is not measured.

labor.older-employment.name: Share of people 62 to 66 who are working
labor.older-employment.unit: percent of people 62 to 66 who are employed (about)
labor.older-employment.source: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2020-2024 5-year, table B23001 (sex by age by employment status), employed over the population for ages 62 to 64 plus two-fifths of ages 65 to 69 (the two single years 65 and 66), men and women together (https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b23001.dat). ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the 65 and 66 part assumes the five years from 65 to 69 are equally populated and equally employed, because the Census Bureau publishes no single-year age cut in this table.
labor.older-employment.note: Covers the 50 states, D.C. and Puerto Rico. The drift keeps the earlier judged settings and is not measured.

farmland.developed-acres.name: Farmland lost to development each year
farmland.developed-acres.unit: acres of farm and ranch land converted to urban, highly developed or low-density residential use a year
farmland.developed-acres.shortUnit: acres of farmland developed a year
farmland.developed-acres.source: American Farmland Trust, Farms Under Threat: The State of the States (2020), Appendix III: agricultural land converted to urban and highly developed or low-density residential use from 2001 to 2016, by state (https://farmlandinfo.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2020/09/AFT_FUT_StateoftheStates_rev.pdf), divided by the 15 years. The 48 contiguous states' rows sum to 10,932,000 acres: 728,800 acres a year.
farmland.developed-acres.note: A yearly average over 2001 to 2016, the latest statewide reading of farmland lost to development; the state and local purchase-of-easement programs then running are already in it. Alaska and Hawaii are left out because the study mapped only the contiguous states, and D.C. and the territories because it did not cover them; those places are unknown and never zero. The drift is judged.

water.irrigation-groundwater.name: Groundwater pumped for irrigation
water.irrigation-groundwater.unit: million gallons a day of fresh groundwater withdrawn for irrigation
water.irrigation-groundwater.shortUnit: million gallons a day of groundwater pumped for irrigation
water.irrigation-groundwater.source: US Geological Survey, Estimated Use of Water in the United States, County-Level Data for 2015, version 2.0 (Dieter and others, 2018, https://doi.org/10.5066/F7TB15V5), fresh groundwater withdrawals for irrigation (IR-WGWFr) summed by state. The 50 states and Puerto Rico total 57,208 million gallons a day.
water.irrigation-groundwater.note: 2015 is the latest year the Geological Survey compiled for every county. D.C. and the Virgin Islands pumped no groundwater for irrigation, and Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands and American Samoa are not in the compilation; those places are left out and never zero. The drift is judged.

farmland.value-per-acre.name: Farm real estate value per acre
farmland.value-per-acre.unit: dollars per acre, farmland and buildings on farms (2025)
farmland.value-per-acre.shortUnit: dollars an acre of farm real estate
farmland.value-per-acre.source: USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service, Land Values 2024 Summary (August 2025), farm real estate average value per acre, 2025 (https://www.nass.usda.gov/Publications/Todays_Reports/reports/land0825.pdf). Delaware's 2025 value is published; its 2024 value is withheld.
farmland.value-per-acre.note: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE for the eight places NASS does not survey (Alaska, Hawaii, D.C. and the five territories): the U.S. average, $4,350 an acre. The drift is judged.

housing.rental-supply.name: Share of homes that are rented
housing.rental-supply.unit: percent of occupied homes that are renter-occupied
housing.rental-supply.source: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2024 1-year, table B25003 Tenure (https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2024/table-based-SF/data/1YRData/acsdt1y2024-b25003.dat): renter-occupied over occupied housing units. Nation: 34.7%.
housing.rental-supply.note: Rent stabilization's measured loss of rental homes (Diamond, McQuade and Qian 2019: 15% among covered landlords) moves this share, so the web applies the covered buildings' loss to the whole place, the upper end of what the study found. The American Community Survey does not cover Guam, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa or the Northern Mariana Islands; those places are unknown and never zero. The drift is judged.

housing.renter-moves.name: Share of renters who moved in the past year
housing.renter-moves.unit: percent of people in renter-occupied homes who lived in a different home one year earlier
housing.renter-moves.source: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2024 1-year, table B07013 Geographical Mobility in the Past Year by Tenure (https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2024/table-based-SF/data/1YRData/acsdt1y2024-b07013.dat): one minus the people in renter-occupied homes who lived in the same house a year earlier, over all people in renter-occupied homes. Nation: 21.6%.
housing.renter-moves.note: Rent stabilization's measured effect, covered renters 20% less likely to move (Diamond, McQuade and Qian 2019), moves this share. The table covers the fifty states and D.C. only; Puerto Rico and the other territories are unknown and never zero. The drift is judged.

housing.new-large-buildings.name: New apartments in large buildings per 10,000 people
housing.new-large-buildings.unit: housing units authorized by building permits in buildings of five or more units in a year, per 10,000 residents
housing.new-large-buildings.source: U.S. Census Bureau, Building Permits Survey, 2024 annual state estimates (https://www2.census.gov/econ/bps/State/st2024a.txt), units in buildings of 5 units or more, over the American Community Survey 2024 1-year population, table B01003 (https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2024/table-based-SF/data/1YRData/acsdt1y2024-b01003.dat). 442,191 units across the states, D.C. and Puerto Rico: 13.0 per 10,000 residents.
housing.new-large-buildings.note: The survey does not cover Guam, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa or the Northern Mariana Islands; those places are unknown and never zero. The drift is judged.

energy.electricity-price.name: Average price of electricity
energy.electricity-price.unit: average retail price of electricity to all customers (homes, businesses and industry), cents per kilowatt-hour
energy.electricity-price.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, State Electricity Profiles 2024, average retail price (https://www.eia.gov/electricity/state/, read Sept. 29, 2026). U.S. 12.94.
energy.electricity-price.note: D.C. is included. Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands are outside EIA's state profiles and are unknown, never zero. The drift is a PROVISIONAL game value: state prices rose about a quarter from 2020 to 2024.

env.emissions.name: Carbon dioxide from energy, per person
env.emissions.unit: energy-related carbon dioxide emissions per resident, metric tons a year
env.emissions.source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, State Energy Data System, per capita energy-related CO2 emissions, 2024 (CO2_total.xlsx, released June 26, 2026, https://www.eia.gov/state/seds/sep_sum/html/xls/CO2_total.xlsx). U.S. 14.1.
env.emissions.note: Counted where the energy is used, so a state that makes power for its neighbors (Wyoming, North Dakota) carries its emissions. D.C. is included. The territories are outside the State Energy Data System's emission tables and are unknown, never zero. The drift is a PROVISIONAL game value: U.S. emissions per person fell from about 20 metric tons in 2000 to 14 in 2024.

env.litter.name: Litter on roads and public places
env.litter.source: Starts at 100 everywhere, because no survey counts litter state by state in the same way. Keep America Beautiful's 2026 National Litter Study found litter down 34% with about 35 billion pieces still in parks, waterways and public spaces (https://kab.org/litter/litter-study/, read Sept. 29, 2026). The drift is a PROVISIONAL game value.
